title: Casual speech (banmal)
plainEnglish: The informal style you use with close friends, people younger than you, and your partner, made by dropping the polite -요 / -습니다 endings.
whenToUse: Use it once you and the other person have agreed to drop formalities, with people clearly younger than you, with close same-age friends, with your boyfriend/girlfriend, and with little kids. A friend might say '우리 말 놓을까?' (should we drop the formal speech?) before you switch. Example: 폰 봤어? 답장 왜 안 해? (Did you see your phone? Why didn't you reply?)
attachmentRule: Take the polite present form and remove -요: 먹어요 → 먹어, 가요 → 가, 좋아요 → 좋아. For nouns, 학생이에요 → 학생이야 (after a consonant) / 친구예요 → 친구야 (after a vowel). Questions, statements, and suggestions all use the same -아/어 form with intonation doing the work: 갈래? / 갈래 / 같이 가. Commands drop -요 too (가 / 먹어), and 'let's' uses -자 (가자, 먹자). Past stays -았/었어 (먹었어), future -ㄹ 거야 (갈 거야).
contrastWith: 반말 vs 존댓말 (요/습니다 polite speech): same verb, different ending. 어디 가요? is polite, 어디 가? is casual. Using 반말 with a stranger, an older person you just met, or a boss sounds rude or like you're picking a fight, so default to 존댓말 until you've clearly agreed to switch.

examples.ko: 야, 오늘 약속 몇 시야?
examples.en: Hey, what time are we meeting today?

examples.ko: 나 지금 가는 중이야, 5분만 기다려.
examples.en: I'm on my way, just wait five minutes.

examples.ko: 우리 이제 말 편하게 하자, 동갑이잖아.
examples.en: Let's talk casually from now on, we're the same age.

examples.ko: 그거 진짜 웃기지 않냐? ㅋㅋㅋ
examples.en: Isn't that so funny? lol

commonMistakes: Switching to 반말 with someone older or a stranger before they offer — it comes off as disrespectful, so wait until they say it's okay.
Keeping -요 stuck on by habit (가요? to a close friend) — drop it fully, and remember the noun ending becomes -야/-이야, not -예요.

practiceItems.prompt: Make '내일 시간 있어요?' casual (to a close friend)
Say 'I'm a student' in banmal
Suggest 'let's eat together' in banmal

studyOrder: First learn the polite -요 forms, since 반말 is just those with -요 removed.
Practice the noun endings -야 / -이야 and the 'let's' ending -자 separately.
Listen to how friends signal the switch ('말 놓자', '편하게 해') so you know when it's socially safe to use.
beginnerExplanation: 반말 is the relaxed way Koreans talk to people they're close to or younger than. The trick is simple: take the polite sentence and chop off the -요 at the end. 좋아요 becomes 좋아, 어디 가요? becomes 어디 가? Be careful, though — Korean cares a lot about who you're talking to, so you only use 반말 with friends, your partner, kids, or after an older person tells you it's fine. With strangers and elders, stay polite. When in doubt, keep the -요 and listen for the moment someone says '편하게 말해' (talk casually) — that's your green light.

title: -jana: 'you know / as you know'
plainEnglish: You use it to remind someone of something you both already know, or to gently point out a reason they should have realized.
whenToUse: When the listener already knows (or should know) the fact and you're nudging them with it. Great for explaining why you can't do something or correcting a wrong assumption softly. Example: 나 오늘 못 가, 내일 시험 있잖아. (I can't go today — I have an exam tomorrow, remember?)
attachmentRule: Attach -잖아 directly to the verb/adjective stem; add -요 to be polite. Present: 있다 → 있잖아(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁘잖아(요). Past: use -았/었잖아 (갔잖아, 먹었잖아). For nouns: -(이)잖아 → 학생이잖아 (after consonant) / 친구잖아 (after vowel). No irregular sound changes beyond the normal stem.
contrastWith: -잖아 vs -거든(요): -잖아 means 'as you ALREADY know' (shared info), while -거든 introduces info that's NEW to the listener. 'I can't, I'm busy 바쁘잖아' = you knew I was busy; '바쁘거든' = letting you know now (and can sound a bit blunt/defensive).

examples.ko: 왜 또 늦었어? 차 막히는 시간이잖아.
examples.en: Why are you late again? It's rush hour, you know.

examples.ko: 그 카페 주말엔 사람 진짜 많잖아, 평일에 가자.
examples.en: That cafe is super crowded on weekends, you know — let's go on a weekday.

examples.ko: 내가 매운 거 못 먹잖아, 딴 거 시키자.
examples.en: You know I can't eat spicy food — let's order something else.

examples.ko: 어제 내가 말했잖아, 오늘 회식이라고.
examples.en: I told you yesterday, remember — there's a work dinner today.

commonMistakes: Using -잖아 with a brand-new fact the listener couldn't know — it sounds like you're blaming them for not knowing. Use -거든(요) or plain statements instead.
Using -잖아 with a senior/stranger; even with -요 it can feel like 'you should already know this,' so it's mainly for friends and familiar people.

practiceItems.prompt: Remind a friend: 'It's payday today, you know' (월급날)
Point out: 'You promised yesterday, remember' (약속하다)
Politely remind a coworker: 'That meeting is tomorrow, you know' (회의)

studyOrder: Learn it first as 'remember?' — a reminder of shared knowledge.
Practice the past form -았/었잖아 since you'll often remind people of past events.
Contrast it side by side with -거든 so you don't mix up 'you know already' vs 'just so you know'.
beginnerExplanation: -잖아(요) is the 'you know' / 'remember?' ending. You stick it on when you're reminding the other person of something they already know, like 'It's rush hour, you know' or 'I can't eat spicy food, remember?' It makes your reason feel shared rather than like new information. Add -요 to keep it polite (있잖아요), or drop it with friends (있잖아). One caution: don't use it for facts the listener has no way of knowing — that comes across as 'why didn't you know this?' Save -잖아 for stuff you've both got in your heads already.

title: -geodeun: 'just so you know / it's because'
plainEnglish: You use it to give a reason or piece of background info that the listener doesn't know yet, often as a comeback or explanation.
whenToUse: When you're telling someone something new — explaining why, or setting up more to come. Example: 나 오늘 일찍 가야 돼. 부모님 오시거든. (I have to leave early today — my parents are coming over, you see.) In texts it often answers a 'why?' with a touch of attitude: 그냥 좀 바쁘거든.
attachmentRule: Attach -거든 to the plain stem; add -요 for politeness. Present: 가다 → 가거든(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁘거든(요). Past: -았/었거든 (먹었거든, 갔거든). Future/plan: -(으)ㄹ 거거든 (갈 거거든). Nouns: -(이)거든(요) → 학생이거든요 / 친구거든요. Sentence-final intonation falls; it commonly sets up a follow-up sentence.
contrastWith: -거든 vs -잖아: -거든 gives NEW info ('just so you know'), -잖아 recalls SHARED info ('as you know'). Also vs -아서/-니까 (reason): those connect inside one sentence (바빠서 못 가), while -거든 ends the sentence and adds a 'here's the backstory' feel. Standalone -거든(요) can sound mildly sassy/defensive, so tone matters.
sentenceFrames: 사실 나 ___ 거든 (Actually, I ___, you see)

examples.ko: 나 그 드라마 벌써 다 봤거든, 스포 하지 마.
examples.en: I've already finished that drama, you see, so no spoilers.

examples.ko: 오늘은 좀 일찍 들어가야 돼. 내일 출근해야 하거든.
examples.en: I have to head home early today — I've got work tomorrow, you see.

examples.ko: 사실 나 그 사람이랑 아는 사이거든. 소개해 줄까?
examples.en: Actually I know that person — want me to introduce you?

examples.ko: 왜 화났냐고? 네가 약속 또 깼거든.
examples.en: Why am I mad? Because you broke your promise again, that's why.

commonMistakes: Using -거든 for info the listener already knows — that's -잖아's job; -거든 should feel like fresh news.
Overusing standalone -거든요 with seniors: the slightly defensive tone can read as 'well, FYI…', so soften with a full reason in formal settings.

practiceItems.prompt: Explain (new info): 'I have to leave early, I have plans' (약속 있다)
practiceItems.ko: 나 일찍 가야 돼, 약속 있거든.
practiceItems.answer: 나 일찍 가야 돼, 약속 있거든.

practiceItems.prompt: Tell a friend (new info): 'I already ate' (먹다)
Politely explain to a coworker: 'I'm a bit busy right now, you see' (바쁘다)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'just so you know / here's why' — info the listener didn't have.
Practice using it to set up a second sentence (reason → then what you'll do).
Compare it directly with -잖아 (new vs shared info) to lock in the difference.
beginnerExplanation: -거든(요) is how you drop new background info on someone — 'just so you know.' If a friend asks why you're leaving early, you say 내일 일찍 출근하거든 (because I have early work tomorrow, you see). It often leads into a second sentence that explains what happens next. Think of -잖아 and -거든 as a pair: -잖아 is 'as you already know,' -거든 is 'something you didn't know.' Add -요 to be polite. Heads up: said all by itself with a sharp tone, -거든요 can sound a little sassy ('well, FYI'), so among friends it's playful, but with elders soften it with a full explanation.

title: -deorago: 'I noticed / turns out'
plainEnglish: You use it to report something you personally saw, felt, or discovered in the past — sharing a firsthand impression.
whenToUse: When you're recounting something you directly experienced and it struck you. Perfect for reviews and gossip. Example: 그 집 가 봤는데 생각보다 비싸더라고. (I went to that place and it was pricier than I expected, turns out.) Used a ton when telling friends about food, people, or places you tried.
attachmentRule: Attach -더라고 to the plain stem; add -요 for politeness. Present-experience: 비싸다 → 비싸더라고(요), 있다 → 있더라고(요). Past (already happened before you noticed): -았/었더라고 (갔더라고요 = turns out they had gone). Nouns: -(이)더라고(요) → 진짜 맛집이더라고요. Key restriction: for your OWN direct observation. With first-person feelings, only inner states work (나 그때 진짜 떨리더라고 = I was so nervous then).
contrastWith: -더라고 vs plain past -았/었어: plain past just states a fact (비쌌어 = it was expensive). -더라고 adds 'and I noticed it myself / it stood out to me,' giving an eyewitness, slightly surprised flavor. Also vs -대(요) (hearsay): -더라고 = I saw it; -대 = I heard it from someone.
sentenceFrames: 가 보니까 ___ 더라고 (When I went, it was ___, turns out)
그 사람 ___ 더라고요 (That person was ___, I noticed)
막상 해 보니까 ___ 더라고 (Once I actually tried it, it was ___)

examples.ko: 거기 분위기 진짜 좋더라고, 데이트하기 딱이야.
examples.en: The vibe there was really nice, turns out — perfect for a date.

examples.ko: 배민으로 시켰는데 생각보다 빨리 오더라고요.
examples.en: I ordered on Baemin and it came faster than I expected, actually.

examples.ko: 새로 온 팀장님 되게 꼼꼼하시더라고.
examples.en: The new team lead is really meticulous, I noticed.

examples.ko: 월세가 생각보다 너무 비싸더라고, 그래서 좀 더 외곽으로 알아봤어.
examples.en: The rent was way pricier than I thought, so I looked a bit further out.

commonMistakes: Using -더라고 for things you only heard about — if you didn't witness it yourself, use -대(요) (hearsay) instead.
Saying 나 똑똑하더라고 (I'm smart, I noticed) — you can't 'observe' your own permanent traits this way; -더라고 with 'I' works only for inner feelings/states you experienced (떨리더라고, 좋더라고).

practiceItems.prompt: Report from a visit: 'The food there was really good, turns out' (맛있다)
Tell a coworker you noticed: 'The new cafe is always crowded' (사람 많다)
practiceItems.ko: 새로 생긴 카페 항상 사람 많더라고요.
practiceItems.answer: 새로 생긴 카페 항상 사람 많더라고요.

practiceItems.prompt: Share your feeling: 'I was really nervous then' (떨리다)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I saw/felt it firsthand, and here's my take.'
Practice pairing it with 가 보니까 / 해 보니까 (when I went/tried) to frame the experience.
Compare -더라고 (I witnessed) with -대 (I heard) so you report sources correctly.
beginnerExplanation: -더라고(요) is your 'firsthand report' ending. When you've personally seen, tried, or felt something, you use it to tell others your impression: 거기 진짜 좋더라고 (turns out that place is really nice). It carries a little 'I noticed this myself, and it kind of surprised me' feeling, which is why Koreans use it constantly for reviewing restaurants, cafes, and people. Add -요 to be polite. Two rules to remember: only use it for things YOU witnessed (for stuff you just heard, use -대), and don't use it to describe your own personality — only your own feelings, like 떨리더라고 (I was nervous).

title: -na boda: 'I guess / it seems'
plainEnglish: You use it to make a guess based on some evidence you're seeing or hearing right now — 'it looks like / I guess so.'
whenToUse: When you infer something from a clue, not direct knowledge. Example: 답장 없는 거 보니까 바쁜가 봐. (Going by the no-reply, I guess they're busy.) Super common for guessing about other people's situations and feelings without being pushy.
attachmentRule: Verbs (action): stem + -나 보다 → 오다 → 오나 보다, 먹다 → 먹나 보다 (past: 먹었나 보다). Adjectives & 이다 (state): stem + -(으)ㄴ가 보다 → 좋다 → 좋은가 보다, 바쁘다 → 바쁜가 보다, 학생이다 → 학생인가 보다. In speech people very often just say -나 봐 for both (좋나 봐 is widely used colloquially). Conjugate 보다 normally: 봐(요), 봐서, 봤어.
contrastWith: -나 보다 vs -것 같다: both mean 'seems,' but -나 보다 is an inference from outside evidence about OTHER people/situations (그 집 잘되나 봐 = looks like that shop's doing well, judging by the crowd). -것 같다 is a broader, softer personal opinion that can also be about yourself (나 감기 걸린 것 같아). You normally don't use -나 보다 about your own clear feelings.
sentenceFrames: ___ 나 봐 (I guess they ___ / it seems they ___)

examples.ko: 읽고 답이 없네, 바쁜가 봐.
examples.en: They read it and didn't reply — I guess they're busy.

examples.ko: 사람들이 줄 선 거 보니까 거기 맛집인가 봐.
examples.en: Going by the line, I guess that place is really good.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 표정 보니까 일 때문에 스트레스 많이 받나 봐.
examples.en: From their face lately, I guess work is stressing them out a lot.

examples.ko: 불 꺼져 있는 거 보니까 다들 퇴근했나 봐요.
examples.en: The lights are off, so I guess everyone's gone home.

commonMistakes: Choosing the wrong connector: verbs take -나 보다, adjectives/이다 take -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (좋나 보다 is colloquial but 좋은가 봐 is the textbook-correct form).
Using -나 보다 about your own obvious feelings (나 배고프나 봐 sounds odd) — you know your own state, so use -것 같다 or just state it.

practiceItems.prompt: Guess from evidence: 'I guess it's raining outside' (비 오다)
Infer about a coworker: 'I guess the new place is expensive' (비싸다)
Guess about a friend: 'I guess they already left' (가다, past)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I guess, based on a clue I can see/hear.'
Drill the verb (-나) vs adjective/이다 (-(으)ㄴ가) split with a few example pairs.
Compare with -것 같다 so you know when it's an evidence-based guess about others vs a general soft opinion.
beginnerExplanation: -나 보다 is how you make an educated guess from a clue in front of you. You see a long line at a restaurant and say 맛집인가 봐 (I guess it's a good spot); someone isn't texting back and you say 바쁜가 봐 (I guess they're busy). It's mostly for guessing about other people or situations, not your own feelings — you already know how you feel. One small grammar point: action verbs use -나 보다 (오나 봐), while adjectives and 이다 use -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (좋은가 봐), though in fast speech you'll hear -나 봐 used loosely for everything. Just conjugate 보다 like a normal verb at the end: 봐, 봐요.

title: -neunde: soft, open-ended ending
plainEnglish: Ending a sentence on -는데(요) leaves it gently hanging, softening a reply, hinting at a 'but…', or inviting the other person to react.
whenToUse: When you want to sound less blunt — answering, mild disagreement, leaving room for a response. Example: 지금은 좀 바쁜데요… (I'm a little busy right now… [so maybe later?]). Also for a surprised/impressed reaction: 오, 잘하는데? (Oh, you're pretty good!). Hugely useful for polite refusals and soft pushback at work.
attachmentRule: Verbs & 있다/없다: stem + -는데(요) → 가다 → 가는데(요), 먹다 → 먹는데(요), 있다 → 있는데(요). Adjectives & 이다: stem + -(으)ㄴ데(요) → 좋다 → 좋은데(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁜데(요), 학생이다 → 학생인데(요). Past (all): -았/었는데(요) → 갔는데(요), 먹었는데(요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -ㄴ데 (멀다 → 먼데요, 길다 → 긴데요). Trailing intonation rises or trails off to create the soft, open feel.
contrastWith: Sentence-final -는데(요) (soft, trailing) vs connective -는데 (mid-sentence 'but/and' that links two clauses: 비싼데 맛있어 = it's pricey but tasty). Same form, but the ending version stops there to leave things open. Vs flat -아/어요: 바빠요 is a hard 'I'm busy'; 바쁜데요… softens it into 'I'm kind of busy (so…)', much friendlier for declining.
sentenceFrames: 지금은 좀 ___ 는데요… (It's a bit ___ right now, so…)
어, 생각보다 ___ 는데? (Oh, that's more ___ than I expected!)

examples.ko: 그 날은 제가 선약이 있는데요, 다른 날은 어때요?
examples.en: I have other plans that day… how about another day?

examples.ko: 어? 너 노래 진짜 잘하는데?
examples.en: Huh? You're actually really good at singing!

examples.ko: 음… 그 가격은 좀 부담스러운데요.
examples.en: Hmm… that price is a little much for me, though.

examples.ko: 저는 이미 다 끝냈는데요? 안 받으셨어요?
examples.en: I already finished it all, though? You didn't get it?

commonMistakes: Mixing up the verb (-는데) and adjective (-(으)ㄴ데) forms: 좋는데 is wrong → 좋은데(요); 바쁘는데 is wrong → 바쁜데(요).
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop: 멀는데요 is wrong → 먼데요; 길는데요 → 긴데요.

practiceItems.prompt: Softly decline: 'I'm a little busy right now…' (바쁘다)
React, impressed: 'Oh, this is pretty tasty!' (맛있다)
Soft pushback: 'I already sent it, though' (보내다, past)

studyOrder: Learn the soft 'trailing off' feel first — it's the politeness superpower of casual Korean.
Drill verb -는데 vs adjective -(으)ㄴ데 and the ㄹ-drop with a few pairs.
Then notice the connective use mid-sentence ('but/and') so you recognize both jobs of the same form.
beginnerExplanation: -는데(요) is one of the most useful endings for sounding natural and polite. Instead of giving a hard, flat answer, you let the sentence trail off, which feels softer and invites the other person to respond. 'I'm busy' as 바빠요 sounds final, but 바쁜데요… feels like 'I'm kind of busy, so maybe we figure something out.' It's also a great reaction when you're pleasantly surprised: 잘하는데? (oh, you're good!). Watch the form: action verbs and 있다/없다 take -는데, while adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ데, and ㄹ-ending stems drop the ㄹ (멀다 → 먼데요). The same shape also works mid-sentence as a gentle 'but,' so you'll see it everywhere.

title: -eulge: 'I'll (do it), promise'
plainEnglish: You use it to announce what YOU will do, usually as a promise or a response to the listener — 'I'll do it / I'll take care of it.'
whenToUse: First person only, reacting to the situation or the other person. Example: 나 먼저 갈게, 이따 연락해. (I'll head out first — text me later.) All over KakaoTalk: 곧 갈게요, 확인하고 답장할게요. Shows you're committing to the action for the listener's benefit.
attachmentRule: After a vowel or ㄹ: -ㄹ게(요) → 가다 → 갈게(요), 만들다 → 만들게(요) (ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ, no doubling). After other consonants: -을게(요) → 먹다 → 먹을게(요), 읽다 → 읽을게(요). ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들을게(요); ㅂ-irregular: 돕다 → 도울게(요). Pronounced [ㄹ께]. First person subject only; no past form.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ게(요) vs -(으)ㄹ래(요): -ㄹ게 is a one-sided promise/decision made FOR or in response to the listener (내가 살게 = I'll pay). -ㄹ래 expresses your own preference or asks the other's (나 집에 갈래 = I want to go home / 갈래? = wanna go?). Also vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (plain future plan): 갈 거예요 just states a plan; 갈게요 feels like a promise responding to you.
sentenceFrames: 먼저 ___ 고 있을게 (I'll be ___ ahead of you)

examples.ko: 이번 커피는 내가 살게, 너 지난번에 샀잖아.
examples.en: I'll get the coffee this time — you paid last time.

examples.ko: 집 도착하면 톡할게요!
examples.en: I'll text you on KakaoTalk when I get home!

examples.ko: 그 자료 제가 오늘 안에 정리해서 보낼게요.
examples.en: I'll organize that file and send it by end of day.

examples.ko: 먼저 들어가 있을게, 천천히 와.
examples.en: I'll go in and wait — take your time.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)ㄹ게요 with a third person (그 사람이 갈게요 is wrong) — it's strictly 'I/we will.' For others, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
Spelling it -ㄹ께요 in writing — the standard spelling is -ㄹ게요 even though it sounds like [께].

practiceItems.prompt: Promise a friend: 'I'll text you when I arrive' (연락하다)
Tell your boss: 'I'll finish it by today' (끝내다)
Offer: 'I'll listen' / 'I'll hear you out' (듣다, ㄷ-irregular)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I'll do it (for you / in response to you)' — a promise, first person only.
Drill the consonant split (-ㄹ게 vs -을게) and the 듣다→들을게, 돕다→도울게 irregulars.
Contrast with -ㄹ래 (preference) and -ㄹ 거예요 (neutral plan) so the nuance is clear.
beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ게(요) is how you tell someone what you'll do, like a little promise. You text a friend 도착하면 연락할게 (I'll contact you when I arrive) or tell your boss 오늘 끝낼게요 (I'll finish today). The key feeling is that you're committing to the action partly for the listener — it's responsive, not just a cold statement of plans. Only use it about yourself (or 'we'); for what someone else will do, switch to -(으)ㄹ 거예요. Attach -ㄹ게 after a vowel (갈게) and -을게 after a consonant (먹을게), and note it's pronounced like '께' but you write it 게.

title: -eullae: 'wanna…? / I think I'll…'
plainEnglish: You use it to ask what the other person feels like doing, or to state your own preference/intention casually — 'wanna…?' or 'I'm gonna…'.
whenToUse: Inviting someone or voicing what you'd like. Example: 우리 영화 볼래? (Wanna watch a movie?) / 나 그냥 집에 있을래. (I think I'll just stay home.) The go-to for suggesting hangouts and dates in a relaxed way.
attachmentRule: After a vowel or ㄹ: -ㄹ래(요) → 가다 → 갈래(요), 놀다 → 놀래(요). After other consonants: -을래(요) → 먹다 → 먹을래(요), 앉다 → 앉을래(요). ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들을래(요); ㅂ-irregular: 돕다 → 도울래(요). Question = rising intonation (갈래?), statement = falling (갈래). First/second person; not for stating a third person's wish.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ래(요) vs -(으)ㄹ까(요): -ㄹ래 asks the listener's preference or states yours (영화 볼래? = do you wanna watch?). -ㄹ까 proposes/wonders together (영화 볼까? = shall we watch?). -ㄹ까 feels more 'let's decide together / I'm wondering,' -ㄹ래 feels more 'what do YOU want?'. As a statement, 갈래 = personal will (a bit insistent if overused with elders), so keep it for friends.
sentenceFrames: 나 그냥 ___ 을래 (I think I'll just ___)
뭐 ___ ㄹ래요? (What would you like to ___?)

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 한강 갈래? 날씨 좋대.
examples.en: Wanna go to the Han River this weekend? They say the weather's nice.

examples.ko: 나 오늘 좀 피곤해서 그냥 집에서 쉴래.
examples.en: I'm kind of tired today, so I think I'll just rest at home.

examples.ko: 커피 마실래, 아니면 그냥 갈래?
examples.en: Wanna grab coffee, or just head off?

examples.ko: 뭐 먹을래? 내가 살게.
examples.en: What do you wanna eat? I'll treat.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)ㄹ래요? to invite a senior/boss — it can sound too casual or even pushy; use -(으)시겠어요? or -(으)ㄹ까요? instead.
Using it for a third person's desire (그 사람 갈래요 is wrong) — for that, use 가고 싶어 하다 (그 사람 가고 싶어 해).

practiceItems.prompt: Invite a friend: 'Wanna eat together?' (먹다)
State your preference: 'I think I'll just go home' (가다)
Ask casually: 'Wanna hang out this weekend?' (놀다, ㄹ-stem)

studyOrder: Learn it as the friendly 'wanna…?' for invitations and your own 'I think I'll…'.
Practice the consonant split and the 듣다→들을래, 돕다→도울래 irregulars.
Compare with -ㄹ까 ('shall we / I wonder') so you pick the right invitation nuance.
beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ래(요) is your everyday 'wanna…?' With friends you ask 영화 볼래? (wanna watch a movie?) or 뭐 먹을래? (what do you wanna eat?), and you state your own choice with 나 집에 있을래 (I think I'll stay home). Rising tone makes it a question, falling tone makes it a statement. It's relaxed and friendly, which is exactly why you should NOT aim it at a boss or someone much older — there it can sound too casual or even a little bossy, so use 같이 가실래요? carefully or switch to -ㄹ까요?. Attach -ㄹ래 after a vowel (갈래) and -을래 after a consonant (먹을래).

title: -jyo: 'right? / isn't it?'
plainEnglish: You use it to confirm something you already believe is true and expect the listener to agree with — 'right? / you know how it is.'
whenToUse: Seeking agreement or stating an obvious shared truth. Example: 오늘 진짜 덥죠? (It's really hot today, right?) Great small talk and for politely confirming plans: 내일 두 시 맞죠? (Tomorrow at two, right?). -죠 is just the contracted, very common spoken form of -지요.
attachmentRule: Attach -지(요) / -죠 to the plain stem. Present: 덥다 → 덥지(요)/덥죠, 가다 → 가지(요)/가죠. Past: -았/었죠 → 갔죠, 먹었죠. Nouns: -(이)죠 → 맞죠, 친구죠. As a question (rising tone) it asks for agreement; as a statement (falling) it asserts 'of course/obviously.' Also softens commands/suggestions: 같이 가죠 (let's go, shall we), 그만하시죠 (let's stop).
contrastWith: -죠? vs -잖아(요): -죠? asks the listener to CONFIRM/agree right now ('it's hot, right?'), while -잖아 reminds them of something already known ('it's summer, you know'). Vs plain -아요?: 더워요? is a genuine question (you don't know); 덥죠? assumes you both feel it and just want a nod.
sentenceFrames: 그건 당연히 ___ 죠 (That's obviously ___, of course)

examples.ko: 이 집 닭갈비 진짜 맛있죠?
examples.en: The dak-galbi here is really good, right?

examples.ko: 내일 모임 일곱 시 맞죠?
examples.en: Tomorrow's meetup is at seven, right?

examples.ko: 당연히 제가 도와드려야죠.
examples.en: Of course I should help you.

examples.ko: 날도 좋은데 한잔하러 가시죠.
examples.en: The weather's nice, so let's go grab a drink, shall we.

commonMistakes: Using -죠? when you genuinely don't know the answer — that's a real question, so use -아요?/-어요?. -죠? presumes the listener will agree.
Writing -죠 as -줘 — they're different; -죠 is the -지요 contraction (confirmation), 줘 is 'give (to me).'

practiceItems.prompt: Confirm with a coworker: 'The meeting's at 3, right?' (맞다)
Small talk: 'It's really cold today, right?' (춥다)
Assert (of course): 'Of course it's delicious' (맛있다)

studyOrder: Learn -죠? as the tag question 'right?' that expects a yes.
Then learn the falling-tone statement use ('of course / obviously').
Contrast with -잖아 (reminder) and plain -아요? (real question) to place it precisely.
beginnerExplanation: -지요, almost always shortened to -죠, is the 'right?' ending. You use it when you're pretty sure of something and just want the other person to agree: 오늘 덥죠? (it's hot today, right?) or 내일 두 시 맞죠? (tomorrow at two, right?). With a falling tone it instead means 'of course' — 당연히 제가 사죠 (of course I'll pay). It's friendly and great for small talk and confirming plans. Don't use it when you truly don't know the answer, though; if it's a real question, use -아요?/어요?. And don't confuse the spelling with 줘 (give) — -죠 comes from -지요.

title: -neyo: realization / reaction
plainEnglish: You use it to react to something you've just noticed, learned, or felt in the moment — surprise, admiration, or a fresh realization.
whenToUse: On-the-spot reactions to new info or what's in front of you. Example: 와, 여기 진짜 예쁘네요! (Wow, this place is really pretty!) Perfect for reacting to photos, food, weather, or news a friend just told you. Adds a warm, spontaneous tone.
attachmentRule: Attach -네(요) to the plain stem. Present: 예쁘다 → 예쁘네(요), 많다 → 많네(요), 오다 → 오네(요). Past: -았/었네(요) → 벌써 갔네(요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -네: 멀다 → 머네(요), 살다 → 사네(요). Nouns: -(이)네(요) → 진짜 맛집이네요. Said with a slightly rising, impressed intonation.
contrastWith: -네(요) vs -군(요)/구나: both mark realization, but -네 is the everyday, conversational reaction (especially spoken), while -군요/-구나 sounds a touch more bookish or to-oneself ('ah, I see'). Vs plain -아요: 예뻐요 just describes ('it's pretty'); 예쁘네요 adds 'oh, I'm noticing/reacting to this right now.'
sentenceFrames: 생각보다 ___ 네요 (It's more ___ than I thought)

examples.ko: 사진 보니까 거기 단풍 진짜 예쁘네요.
examples.en: Looking at the photo, the autumn leaves there are really pretty.

examples.ko: 어, 벌써 막차 시간이네. 우리 가야겠다.
examples.en: Oh, it's already last-train time. We'd better go.

examples.ko: 오늘 길 안 막히네, 웬일이지?
examples.en: Traffic's clear today — what's the occasion?

examples.ko: 손맛이 좋으시네요! 이거 직접 만드신 거예요?
examples.en: You're a great cook! Did you make this yourself?

commonMistakes: Using -네요 for facts you already knew — it specifically signals 'I just realized this,' so for known info use plain -아요.
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop: 멀네요 is wrong → 머네요; 살네요 → 사네요.

practiceItems.prompt: React to a photo: 'Wow, the view is really nice!' (좋다)
Notice the time: 'Oh, it's already late' (늦다)
React: 'It's farther than I thought' (멀다, ㄹ-drop)

studyOrder: Learn it as your instant 'oh!' reaction to new info or what you see.
Practice the past -았/었네(요) for noticing things already done (벌써 갔네).
Watch the ㄹ-drop (멀다→머네요) and compare lightly with -군요 (more to-oneself).
beginnerExplanation: -네(요) is the ending you reach for the instant you notice or realize something. See a pretty view and say 예쁘네요!, glance at the clock and say 벌써 늦었네 (oh, it's already late). It carries a warm, spontaneous, slightly impressed feeling, so Koreans use it constantly when reacting to photos, food, or news. The contrast with plain -아요 is subtle but real: 예뻐요 simply states 'it's pretty,' while 예쁘네요 adds 'I'm noticing this right now.' One spelling tip: ㄹ-ending stems drop the ㄹ before -네, so 멀다 becomes 머네요, not 멀네요.

title: -geot gata: 'I think / it seems'
plainEnglish: You use it to soften an opinion or make a guess — 'I think… / it seems like…' — instead of stating things too directly.
whenToUse: Whenever you want to hedge an opinion, prediction, or feeling so you don't sound too blunt. This is everywhere in polite Korean. Example: 이건 좀 어려울 것 같아요. (I think this might be a bit difficult.) Essential for declining, giving feedback at work, and sharing opinions among new acquaintances.
attachmentRule: Pick the modifier by tense/type before 것 같다: verbs — past -(으)ㄴ (먹은 것 같다 = seems they ate), present -는 (먹는 것 같다 = seems they're eating), future/guess -(으)ㄹ (먹을 것 같다 = I think they'll eat). Adjectives & 이다 — present -(으)ㄴ (좋은 것 같다, 학생인 것 같다), guess -(으)ㄹ (좋을 것 같다). 것 같다 is often spoken as 것 같아(요) or 거 같아(요). ㄹ-stems and ㅂ/ㄷ irregulars follow the usual modifier rules (살다→사는, 덥다→더운, 듣다→듣는).
contrastWith: -것 같다 vs -나 보다: -것 같다 is a broad, soft opinion or guess that can include yourself (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 = I think I caught a cold). -나 보다 is specifically an inference from outside evidence about others/situations (감기 걸렸나 봐 = looks like they caught a cold). Vs flat assertion: 별로예요 ('it's not great') is direct, 별로인 것 같아요 ('I think it's not great') is gentler and safer socially.
sentenceFrames: 이건 좀 ___ (으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (I think this might be a bit ___)
그 사람 ___ 는 것 같아 (It seems like they ___)
오늘은 못 ___ (으)ㄹ 것 같은데요 (I don't think I can ___ today…)

examples.ko: 이 옷 나한테 좀 큰 것 같아, 한 사이즈 작은 거 없어요?
examples.en: I think this is a bit big on me — do you have it one size smaller?

examples.ko: 오늘 회식은 못 갈 것 같아요, 집에 일이 좀 있어서요.
examples.en: I don't think I can make the work dinner today — something came up at home.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 좀 바쁜 것 같더라.
examples.en: Seems like they've been pretty busy lately.

examples.ko: 이 정도면 충분할 것 같은데, 어때요?
examples.en: I think this much should be enough — what do you think?

commonMistakes: Using the wrong modifier tense: 먹는 것 같다 (seems eating now) vs 먹은 것 같다 (seems already ate) vs 먹을 것 같다 (I think will eat) — mixing these changes the meaning.
Over-hedging things you actually know firsthand (나 한국 사람인 것 같아 about yourself sounds odd) — use it for opinions/guesses, not certain facts about yourself.

practiceItems.prompt: Soften an opinion: 'I think this is a bit expensive' (비싸다, present adj)
Politely decline: 'I don't think I can go today' (가다, guess)
Guess about now: 'It seems like it's raining' (오다, present verb)

studyOrder: Learn it first as the all-purpose softener 'I think / it seems.'
Drill the three modifiers before 것: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는 (verbs), future/guess -(으)ㄹ.
Compare with -나 보다 (evidence-based, about others) so you choose the right 'seems.'
beginnerExplanation: -것 같다 ('I think / it seems') is maybe the most important softening tool in Korean. Koreans avoid sounding too blunt, so instead of 비싸요 (it's expensive) they often say 비싼 것 같아요 (I think it's a bit expensive), and instead of a flat 'no' they say 못 갈 것 같아요 (I don't think I can go). It works for opinions, predictions, and guesses, and it can be about yourself too (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 = I think I caught a cold). The one fiddly part is the little word before 것: use -는 for what's happening now, -(으)ㄴ for what already happened, and -(으)ㄹ for what you predict. In speech it's usually shortened to 거 같아(요).

title: -eulgeol: 'I bet…' / 'should've…'
plainEnglish: With falling tone it expresses mild regret ('I should have…'); with a guessing tone it makes a confident-ish prediction ('I bet… / probably').
whenToUse: Two everyday uses. Regret about something you didn't do: 아, 어제 그거 살걸. (Ugh, I should've bought that yesterday.) Or a hunch you're fairly sure of: 지금 가면 막힐걸? (If we go now, it'll probably be jammed.) Both are very common in casual chat among young adults.
attachmentRule: Prediction sense (verbs & adjectives): after a vowel/ㄹ -ㄹ걸(요), after a consonant -을걸(요) → 막히다 → 막힐걸(요), 좋다 → 좋을걸(요), 살다 → 살걸(요). Past prediction: -았/었을걸(요) → 갔을걸요 (they probably went). Regret sense (only your own past inaction, no -요, no past form): -(으)ㄹ걸 → 살걸, 갈걸, 먹을걸 (= I should've bought/gone/eaten). ㄷ-irreg 듣다 → 들을걸, ㅂ-irreg 돕다 → 도울걸. Pronounced [껄].
contrastWith: Regret -(으)ㄹ걸 vs -았/었어야 했는데: -ㄹ걸 is the light, spoken 'aw, should've' to yourself; -았어야 했는데 is a fuller 'I really should have…'. Prediction -(으)ㄹ걸(요)? vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요: -ㄹ걸 is a softer hunch you're guessing ('probably, I bet'), -ㄹ 거예요 states a more confident future. Tone tells regret (falling) from prediction (slight rise).
sentenceFrames: 지금 ___ 면 ___ 을걸? (If we ___ now, it'll probably ___)

examples.ko: 아, 어제 표 미리 예매할걸. 지금 다 매진이래.
examples.en: Ugh, I should've booked the tickets yesterday. They say it's all sold out now.

examples.ko: 지금 출발하면 차 엄청 막힐걸?
examples.en: If we leave now, it'll probably be super jammed, I bet.

examples.ko: 걔 그 얘기 들으면 좋아할걸요.
examples.en: They'll probably be happy to hear that, I'd bet.

examples.ko: 그냥 집에 있을걸, 괜히 나왔네.
examples.en: I should've just stayed home — coming out was pointless.

commonMistakes: Using the regret -(으)ㄹ걸 about someone else — it's only for your OWN past inaction; for predictions about others use -(으)ㄹ걸요? with a guessing tone.
Adding -요 or past tense to the regret meaning (살걸요 / 샀을걸 as regret is wrong) — regret stays plain present-shaped -(으)ㄹ걸; -요 and -았을걸 push it into the prediction reading.

practiceItems.prompt: Express regret: 'Ugh, I should've left earlier' (일찍 나오다)
Make a hunch: 'That place is probably closed now' (문 닫다)
Predict politely: 'It'll probably be expensive' (비싸다)

studyOrder: Learn the two senses separately: falling-tone regret ('should've') and guessing-tone prediction ('I bet').
For regret, lock in: your own past inaction only, plain -(으)ㄹ걸, no -요.
For prediction, practice -(으)ㄹ걸요? and the past -았/었을걸(요), and contrast with the firmer -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ걸 wears two hats depending on your tone. Said with a sighing, falling tone, it's regret — 'I should've': 일찍 나올걸 (I should've left earlier), 그거 살걸 (I should've bought that). Said with a slight upward, guessing tone, it's a confident hunch — 'I bet / probably': 지금 가면 막힐걸? (it'll probably be jammed if we go now). Young Koreans use both constantly in chat. Two things to remember: the regret version is only about your own past inaction and stays plain (no -요), while the prediction version can add -요 to be polite (비쌀걸요) and can go past tense (갔을걸 = they probably went). It's spelled 걸 but sounds like '껄'.
